archetype.name: Super Bowl Contender (pass-efficiency engine)
archetype.definition: A 5-0 team whose league-best net EPA, passing efficiency and pass protection would support a top seed even after the close-game luck fades.

report.headline: The real thing this time, but the depth chart is starting to fray.
report.take:
Last year's 49ers went 12-5 on a 15th-ranked net EPA and 2.62 wins over expected, which made them a fortunate team rather than a great one. This year's 5-0 start looks different. They rank 1st in net EPA (0.259), 1st in offensive success rate and 1st in pass EPA per play (0.389), with a defense 4th in EPA allowed. The offense's 0.187 EPA per play is right at the level of the 2023 group that led the league. The record is built on play quality, not only on bounces.

The passing game runs through the protection. Purdy has been pressured on 10.2% of dropbacks and sacked on 1.9%, both best in the league, while holding the ball 3.05 seconds. That is time to let Shanahan's concepts develop. The run game is solid rather than special: 3rd in yards before contact and 5th in success rate, but 13th in EPA. On defense the identity is no explosives. They rank 1st in both explosive-pass and explosive-rush rate allowed and 4th against the run. The trade-off is a middling pass rush (16th in pressure rate) and soft underneath coverage, 21st in short-pass EPA.

Two things in the numbers deserve some caution. First, the opponent sequence flatters the offense. Its two monster passing games (23.3 and 22.9 pass EPA) came against Miami and Arizona, whose defenses now rank 28th and 29th. Against Denver (7th) the pass EPA fell to 8.5, and in Seattle (2nd) it was negative, with three turnovers and the only three sacks allowed all year. Second, the 2.03 wins over expected and a perfect one-score record mean the ARI and SEA wins could have gone either way. A +4 takeaway day bailed out the Seattle game. Special teams (29th) are a steady leak.

The bigger near-term issue is attrition. Deebo Samuel (20 targets) is out for at least a couple of weeks, and Christian Kirk is on IR. On defense, Sigle (88% snaps) is out, Greenlaw is suspended for Washington, Wallow is out, and Bosa, who has played only two games, is a 'has a chance.' The pass game will narrow to Evans, Kittle and McCaffrey. A defense that already gives up the underneath stuff loses its starting safety and its best linebacker for a week. Even so, the efficiency base is strong enough that this remains a top-two NFC team.

strengths.title: Best pass protection in football
strengths.body: San Francisco has allowed three sacks in five games and leads the league in both pressure rate and sack rate allowed, despite a long time to throw. That combination means the line is holding up rather than Purdy just getting rid of it fast. Pass protection is one of the stickier unit traits, though Seattle showed a top defense can still get home.

strengths.title: League-best passing efficiency
strengths.body: At 0.389 EPA per dropback and a 51.9% offensive success rate, the Purdy passing game is the league's most efficient. It is helped by soft opponents (Miami and Arizona produced most of the pass EPA). Still, it matches the offense's 2023 peak, and history says this scheme sustains it. Expect some regression toward the merely elite as the defenses get tougher.

strengths.title: Nothing gets over the top
strengths.body: The defense ranks 1st in both explosive pass and explosive rush rate allowed and 4th in rush EPA. It makes offenses earn every drive in small chunks. A 6th-ranked red-zone TD rate finishes the job. A defense that cuts off big plays tends to hold up, though it is the safety and linebacker depth now being tested.

concerns.title: Defensive back seven thinning out
concerns.body: Sigle (88% snaps) is out and Greenlaw is suspended for Week 6. Wallow is out for weeks, and Bosa has played only two games. This defense already concedes underneath (21st in short-pass EPA) and gets just middling pressure. Losing a starting safety and linebacker hits exactly that soft spot. Most of it is short-term, but stacked absences are how a 4th-ranked defense becomes a 15th-ranked one for a month.

concerns.title: Close-game and turnover luck
concerns.body: Two of the five wins came by six or fewer, and the team is 2.03 wins above what its point differential predicts. The Seattle win came despite three giveaways, rescued by four takeaways. Last season's 12-5 was built on the same kind of luck and hid a 15th-ranked net EPA. The difference now is the efficiency underneath, but the close-game edge will not stay perfect.

concerns.title: Offense dipped against good defenses
concerns.body: The two best defenses on the slate held the passing game to 8.5 pass EPA (Denver) and -2 (Seattle). The Seattle game also produced all three sacks allowed and three turnovers. Those are small samples, but the rest of the schedule features Minnesota (1st on defense), Seattle again, Atlanta, the Chargers and Kansas City. Losing Deebo narrows the answers against those units. Special teams, 29th in EPA, add a hidden tax in tight games.

trend.note: Wins every week and covers in four of five, but the margin of dominance shrank as opponents improved. A 22-point blowout of Miami gave way to a 10-point win over Denver and a three-point escape in Seattle, where the offense had its worst game.

nextGame.headline: Washington's leaky pass defense is built for Purdy and Kittle.
nextGame.body:
Washington is a run-stopping, pass-allowing defense, and that matches San Francisco's profile well. The Commanders rank 7th in rush EPA allowed and have held lead backs 4.1 PPR points under their averages. Against the pass they are 25th in EPA, and offenses pass on them 6.1 points more often than normal, the 3rd-strongest pass funnel. Tight ends have feasted, scoring 10.7 PPR over their averages, the worst mark in the league. Washington also converts almost nothing into stops near the goal line, allowing touchdowns on 83% of red-zone trips, last in the league. Its 27th-ranked sack rate gives little hope of disrupting the best protection in football. On the other side, Washington's offense is 27th in success rate and 21st in rush EPA, which plays into a defense that strangles the run.

Availability cuts both ways but leans toward San Francisco. Washington is without safety Nick Cross (99% snaps), Butler and Owens, plus Diggs, Omenihu and corner Trey Amos. That secondary is in shambles against a team that wants to throw. Daniels is back under center after a Week 4 Mariota start, and Mariota is out. San Francisco has to play without Greenlaw (suspended), Sigle and Deebo. Bosa is uncertain, and Juszczyk and Thompson could return. The eight days of rest and a home game help.

keyMatchups.title: Kittle against a broken safety group
keyMatchups.body: Washington has been the worst defense in the league against tight ends, and three of its safeties are out, including the 99%-snap Cross. With Deebo and Kirk sidelined, Kittle's 28 targets in five games should climb. Expect him to be the volume and red-zone outlet. This is the cleanest edge on the board.

keyMatchups.title: Red zone: elite offense vs worst defense
keyMatchups.body: San Francisco scores 30.8 a game, and Washington lets 83% of red-zone trips end in touchdowns, last in the league. Drives that stall into field goals elsewhere should finish here. That is the main path to the 49ers clearing their implied total.

keyMatchups.title: McCaffrey into a stout front
keyMatchups.body: Washington's run defense is the healthy part of its unit, 7th in rush EPA and 2nd at holding lead backs under their averages. San Francisco's run game is efficient by success rate but only 13th in EPA. Expect the yards to come through the air, with McCaffrey's value in the 25-target receiving role.

nextGame.watch: Whether Bosa plays. Without him, Greenlaw and Sigle, the short middle of the field is where Daniels can keep Washington close enough to sneak inside the 7.5.

restOfSeason.body:
The underlying engine, elite protection plus the league's most efficient passing game, is sustainable. The 2023 version of this offense held a similar level all year. What will regress is the margin around it. A perfect one-score record and a turnover edge will not hold, and the schedule ahead is defense-heavy: Atlanta (7th), Minnesota (1st), Seattle (2nd), the Chargers (6th) and Kansas City. Those are the units that dented this offense in Weeks 4 and 5. Points per game should settle from 30.8 into the high 20s.

The defense is the swing piece. Healthy, its no-explosives approach plays against anybody. The current run of injuries to the safety, linebackers and Bosa is the main threat to a top seed. With a two-game lead in the NFC West and soft division games against the Rams and Cardinals, the 49ers should win the division and remain a top-two NFC seed.
swingFactors: Bosa's calf and the safety/linebacker depth
Offense against the Minnesota, Seattle and KC defenses

bets.reason: Washington allows tight ends 10.7 PPR over their averages (32nd) and is missing three safeties, including its 99%-snap starter. Deebo and Kirk are out, which concentrates targets on Kittle.

The spread and total imply about 29 for San Francisco. They average 30.8 against a Washington defense that is 25th in pass EPA, allows 29.8 a game and gives up red-zone touchdowns at the league's worst rate. They also face a weak pass rush (27th in sack rate).

The net EPA gap is huge (1st vs 25th), San Francisco is 4-1 ATS, and Washington's secondary is depleted. Home wins have come by 22, 6 and 10 points. Short-handed linebackers and safeties plus bad special teams keep it from being a stronger play at the hook.
Washington's strength is its run defense (7th in rush EPA, 2nd vs lead backs), and it is a strong pass funnel. The 49ers' rush EPA is only 13th, so the game plan should tilt to the air.

confidence.note: Five games and a soft early slate, plus a stack of injuries reshaping both sides of the ball.
